q: Explain the economics of holding ageing stock on a restaurant list: markup structure, turns, and carrying cost.
accept: sliding scale or cash margin markup with turns and carrying cost
coefficient pricing turns per year and the capital tied up in ageing stock
flat multiples fail at the top so use cash gross profit and watch inventory turns
balance high-turn wines against a limited share of capital in cellaring
ans: Three levers. Markup: a flat multiple prices cheap wines sensibly and expensive ones absurdly, so serious lists use a sliding coefficient or a cash-margin floor — a fixed sum of gross profit per bottle above a threshold — which makes the fine end sellable and raises absolute profit even as percentage margin falls. Turns: a wine bought and sold four times a year earns its shelf space four times over, while a case of Barolo lying quietly for eight years earns nothing at all until it moves, so cellaring is a capital allocation decision rather than a hobby. Carrying cost: cash tied up, insurance, cellar space, and shrinkage through breakage, theft and by-the-glass oxidation — set against appreciation and the blunt fact that mature wine cannot be bought later at a price you will enjoy. The reconciliation is a barbell: high-turn wines fund the operation while a deliberately capped share of capital sits in ageing stock whose replacement cost is climbing faster than the cost of holding it.
exp: Beverage directors are hired for palate and fired for inventory. The mature depth that makes a list famous is bought with money that could have been turning four times a year, so the defence of that decision has to be financial, not romantic — and it has to name a cap.

q: Explain why Alsace's 'grand cru' system underperforms commercially despite its 51 sites.
accept: too many crus inconsistent quality producers ignore it varietal confusion
dilution of the concept and top houses opting out
ans: Rapid expansion diluted the concept, quality varies widely within crus, and leading houses (Trimbach, Hugel) decline to use it — leaving the market unconvinced
exp: A market-analysis question as much as a wine one.
